shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner on an airline flight, on radar vectors for a visual approach to a large airport. Clear visual conditions, daytime.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring.

What happened. On the downwind leg, air traffic control told the crew to descend to 4,000 ft and turn right to heading 170. The captain set both on the mode control panel; the first officer read back and confirmed the numbers. Heading mode did not engage at first, and the turn began about 35 seconds late. Meanwhile the first officer was looking out for traffic and checking the airspace chart, which showed 4,000 ft as safe there. In the turn, the controller gave further turns to 180 and 210 and asked if the crew needed assistance, which confused the first officer, as everything seemed normal. The controller then gave a low altitude alert for a minimum vectoring altitude of 4,200 ft, noting the aircraft was at 4,600 ft, but did not say to stop the descent. The first officer understood that the minimum ahead was 4,200 ft and that the aircraft, above it, turning and cleared to 4,000 ft, was fine. The crew had no means of seeing minimum vectoring altitudes. The controller then said, in a raised voice, "Turn your plane now." The aircraft was already in an established turn; the crew judged more bank would risk an unusual attitude. The captain held the bank and continued the turn.
safe_outcome: Air traffic control vectored the aircraft off the approach and back round for another intercept, and it landed without further incident. During the turn, air traffic control had given traffic information on a converging aircraft about 2 miles away, at 11 o'clock and 1,000 ft below, while this aircraft was turning right, away from it. There were no TCAS or ground proximity alerts. No one was hurt and no aircraft was damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
bracket_fill: [climbing / descending / crossing] = crossing; [this aircraft] = this aircraft
notes: Removed under rule 3: both 'Cause' sections; the captain's 'my unintentional error', 'I take full responsibility', 'at no point was the flight ever in an unsafe condition' and praise of the first officer; the captain's characterisations of the controller ('did a poor job', 'stressed tone', 'made it worse'); the first officer's 'accidental mistake' and the later discussion of controller workload, unpublished minimum vectoring altitudes and recommendations. Kept as facts at the time: the late turn, the first officer's check of the numbers in the windows, the first officer's reading of the low altitude alert and the reason for it (no instruction to stop the descent or change the clearance), the lack of minimum vectoring altitude information on the flight deck, and the crew's reason for not increasing bank. Moved to the safe ending (rule 5, deviation D4): the ATC traffic information on the converging aircraft, and the absence of TCAS and ground proximity alerts. Left out: ATC's remark after the event that the flight might have come close to the minimum vectoring altitude (an assessment, not an event). Removed under rule 6: arrival and fix names, the runway and the airport. Judgement calls: the captain says heading mode was selected late and the first officer says it did not engage at first, so the text says it 'did not engage at first'; the two accounts give the 'Turn your plane now' call and the traffic call in different orders, so no order is stated. The aircraft's speed (190 knots, as assigned) was left out for length. Bracket 'crossing' because the traffic reported was converging from the left while this aircraft turned and descended.
